pronunciation.approximation: TROY-ah, with the stress on the final syllable and a long ā.
pronunciation.note: Greek Τροία bears the stress on the final syllable with a long diphthongal ending — Troíā — and Latin Troia keeps both the vowels and the fame. The form was already a place-name before it was a story: Hittite records call the land Wilusa, which most scholars now connect to (W)ilios, Troy's other Greek name.

domains.title: The City of Story
domains.subtitle: Siege, Horse, and the Mother of Empires
domains.lead: Troíā is the city that fell once and rose forever: ten years of siege made it the template of Western war narrative, and its survivors — in Roman myth — sailed west to found the lineage of Rome itself. Every empire since has wanted to be Troy's heir rather than its conqueror.

cards.name: The Walls
cards.desc: Built by Poseidṓn and Apóllōn — walls only a trick could breach.

cards.name: The Horse
cards.desc: Odysseus' stratagem: the gift that is a breach, the original Trojan horse.

cards.name: The Ten Years
cards.desc: The Iliad covers fifty days; the full siege cycle filled the entire Epic Cycle.

cards.name: The Exiles
cards.desc: Aeneas carries his father and his gods out of the fire — Troy's fall as Rome's first chapter.

symbols.name: The wooden horse
symbols.meaning: Ingenuity against fortification; the gift that conceals its content

symbols.name: The Scaean Gate
symbols.meaning: The western gate where the heroes fought and the horse entered

symbols.name: The Palladium
symbols.meaning: The heaven-fallen image of Athēnā on which the city's safety depended

symbols.name: The Scamander (Xanthos)
symbols.meaning: The river of the plain, deity and battlefield — where Achilles choked the waters with the dead until the river itself rose in anger (Iliad 21)

symbols.name: Priam's towers / Pergamos
symbols.meaning: The citadel that outlasted the city in name — the terrace where the altars of Zeus Herkeios and the household gods stood

mythology.lead: The Trojan cycle is the largest story the Greeks told: from the wedding of Pēleús and the Apple of Discord to the Returns of the heroes, it fills eight epics, of which the Iliad and Odyssey are only the surviving heart.

myths.title: The Apple of Discord
myths.text: At the wedding of Pēleús and Thetis, where every god was feasted, Eris arrived uninvited and rolled among the guests a golden apple inscribed 'for the fairest' — and Hēra, Athēnā, and Aphrodítē each claimed it. Zeus, foreseeing the wrath of two losers in any verdict of his own, refused to judge and sent the goddesses to the Trojan prince Páris, exposed as an infant and herding his father's flocks on Mount Ídē. Hēra offered him empire, Athēnā military glory, Aphrodítē the most beautiful woman in the world; he chose the last, and the war became arithmetic. The Cypria, as Proclus summarizes it, makes the mechanism exact: Páris's choice triggers the oath of Tyndareus, the compact under which every former suitor of Helénē is bound to defend her marriage — so one shepherd's preference converts three insulted goddesses into a thousand-ship alliance. Troy's doom was negotiated before its walls were named.

myths.title: Nine Years and a Quarrel
myths.text: A thousand ships mustered at Aulis, where Agamémnōn sacrificed his daughter Iphigéneia for a wind; nine years of raids followed before the Iliad's subject even begins. The tenth year opens with a quarrel inside the Greek camp: Agamémnōn seizes Brisēís from Achilléús, Achilléús withdraws his Myrmidons, and the Greeks begin to die of the absence of one man. The poem covers fifty-one days and never shows the fall: its subject is the chain of deaths the quarrel unlocks — Pátroklos in Achilléús's armor, Héktōr by the Scamander, and behind every duel the city's doom, prophesied and accepted by all the combatants. The war's deepest irony is Homer's structure: he sings one wound in the Greek body — honor — while behind it the real wound, the city, waits untouched. The Iliad ends with Héktōr's ransom, the truce, and the funeral games; everyone knows what comes next, and the knowing is the poem's ache.

myths.title: The Last Night
myths.text: The end the Iliad withholds, the Odyssey and the Aeneid supply. After ten failed years, Odysseus proposes the stratagem: a great wooden horse, hollow, its belly an ambush, left on the shore as an offering to Athēnā while the fleet sails behind Ténedos. The priest Laokóōn hurls his spear into the flank and warns — I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts — and sea-serpents rise from the water and destroy him and his sons, read by the Trojans as the goddess's answer. The prophetess Kassándrā is disbelieved, as always. At night the horse opens: warriors drop to the ground, open the Scaían Gate, and the fleet returns while the city sleeps. Priam is cut down at the altar of Zeus of the Courtyard; the infant Astyanax is thrown from the towers; Menelaos reclaims Helénē; Aineías shoulders his father Anchises and carries his household gods out of the fire. The horse is the myth's perfect machine: a gift that is a breach, an offering that is an army, the wall's conqueror cut from the forest by the wall's besiegers.

myths.title: The Dispersal
myths.text: Greek myth scattered the victors as thoroughly as the defeated. Agamémnōn sailed home to be murdered by Klytaimnḗstrē and Aígisthos in his own hall; Menélaos wandered seven years, touching Egypt; the lesser Aias drowned for his impiety at Athēnā's altar; and Odysseus, the war's author, took ten years for a voyage that should have taken weeks — his nostos the Odyssey itself. The Trojans fared strangely better in memory: Anténōr led a colony to the Adriatic coast; the minority tradition spared Astyanax and rebuilt a new Troy; and above all Aineías, whose westward voyage Virgil's Aeneid turned into the founding journey of Rome — Lavinium, Alba Longa, Rhea Silvia, and the twins. Rome then did what no conqueror had: it adopted the conquered as its mother, and 'Trojan' became, across Europe, a title of glory claimed by the Franks and the Britons alike. The city that fell became the ancestor of everything that claimed to have made it fall.

lore.syncretism: Rome adopted Troy as mother: the Aeneid makes Aeneas' refugees the seed of the Roman people, and Ilium Novum — New Troy — received Roman privileges as a symbolic ancestor. The Middle Ages multiplied the claim: the Franks, the Britons (through Brutus of Troy in Geoffrey of Monmouth), and half the dynasties of Europe forged Trojan genealogies. "Trojan" became a compliment — faithful, brave — even in the languages of the Greeks' heirs.
lore.culturalLegacy: "Trojan horse" is now the universal term for a payload hidden inside a gift — the computing term is simply the myth recompiled. The question "was Troy real?" launched modern archaeology: Schliemann's excavations at Hisarlık (1870s–90s) proved a fortified Bronze Age citadel exactly where Homer put it. The Hittite archives' Wilusa and Taruisa, matched to (W)ilios and Troia by a century of scholarship, made Troy the test case for how myth and document corroborate each other.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Troíā is the city that teaches what walls cannot do. Gods built hers; a story breached them. Every culture that has traced its ancestry to her fall has understood the lesson: the defeated city outlived all its conquerors because it alone became a story that everyone, including its enemies, needed to tell.

Her deepest lesson is the one the victors learned first: that a story is stronger than a wall. The Greeks won the war and spent three thousand years inside the city's aftermath — and Rome, wiser than all of them, simply claimed to be her. Every culture since has faced the same choice at her gate: to besiege the past, or to inherit it.

The Hittite letter and the burned layer do not prove the Iliad — nothing could — but they do the more valuable thing: they give the song an address. Every retelling since has been a kind of excavation, brushing the myth to find the memory underneath, and every excavator has found what Schliemann found: that a story told long enough and loved enough becomes true in the only way that finally matters — people build on it.

Every autumn the plain floods a little, as the Scamander remembers its old bed, and the mound stands in the water-meadow like the ship of the story it carries — nine cities deep, one name, and still unsinkable.

And the plain is quiet now, the way famous battlefields are — which is its own testimony: the war ended, the song did not.

lore.archaeology: Hisarlık in northwest Anatolia preserves nine major settlement layers (Troy I–IX), ca. 3000 BCE–500 CE. The candidates for Homer's city are Troy VI (destroyed ca. 1250 BCE, by earthquake or war) and Troy VIIa (burned ca. 1180 BCE, with sling stones and arrowheads in the destruction debris). UNESCO listed the site in 1998. The "Treasure of Priam" Schliemann smuggled out is now split between Moscow and Istanbul, and the Hittite Tawagalawa letter mentioning a king of Ahhiyawa (Achaeans?) at Millawanda places Greek-Anatolian conflict in the right sea at the right century.
